records.place: Ribeauvillé, with the clos at Hunawihr, Alsace

wine.name: Riesling Clos Sainte Hune
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, as Alsace law asks of any wine labelled with one grape.
wine.sites: Clos Sainte Hune, a small parcel inside the Rosacker Grand Cru on the slope above Hunawihr, held by the family for some two centuries, on limestone.
wine.making: Picked by hand and pressed gently, the wine is fermented dry in stainless steel, with no oak and no malolactic conversion, to keep its acidity whole. It is bottled young and then held in the house's cellars at Ribeauvillé for several years before it is released.
wine.glass: Lime peel, green apple and white peach over crushed limestone and a smoky, saline edge; bone dry, taut and long. Age brings petrol, beeswax, dried lemon and toast.
wine.ageing: Closed and severe for its first decade, it opens slowly after ten years and keeps for thirty and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, never an old one; a wide white wine glass.

label.means: The parcel's name as the label writes it, Ste for Sainte, after the saint of Hunawihr.
The regional appellation: the label names no Grand Cru, though the parcel lies inside the Rosacker.
The grape, and the whole of the wine, as an Alsace varietal label requires.

records.table: From a small family parcel inside the Rosacker Grand Cru at Hunawihr comes Trimbach's Clos Sainte Hune, a Riesling whose label names only Alsace. Fermented bone dry with no oak, it is taut and stony in youth, so offer it with ten years behind it.
records.story: Riquewihr is where the Trimbach story starts: in 1626, by the house's own account, a Trimbach was received as a citizen of the town, and the family's record in wine begins there; the house later made its home at Ribeauvillé, a few kilometres north. Between the two towns lies Hunawihr, named, as the clos is, for Saint Hune, a local saint of the early Middle Ages. The family has held its parcel on the slope above the village for some two centuries and bottled the wine under the saint's name long before Alsace had a law of crus. The appellation Alsace came in 1962 and the Grand Cru tier in 1975, and the hill around the clos was later classified as Grand Cru Rosacker. Trimbach kept that name off the label: the clos was known as itself, and the house held that a cru is a site, not a maker's promise. It made the wine as it made everything else, dry, taut and without oak, and released it only after years in the cellar. The house's Schlossberg has carried Grand Cru since the 2014 vintage, while Clos Sainte Hune has never done so. No Alsace label teaches more plainly that a parcel's own name can say more than its appellation.

others.name: Riesling Cuvée Frédéric Emile
others.note: Riesling from the Geisberg and Osterberg Grand Cru slopes above Ribeauvillé, labelled simply Alsace.

others.name: Gewurztraminer Cuvée des Seigneurs de Ribeaupierre
others.note: A dry Gewurztraminer named for the old lords of Ribeauvillé, drier than the grape's reputation suggests.

others.name: Riesling Réserve
others.note: The house Riesling, and the measure of its dry style.

traps: Clos Sainte Hune lies inside the Rosacker Grand Cru, yet its label names only the appellation Alsace.
The house stands at Ribeauvillé, while Clos Sainte Hune lies at Hunawihr, the next village to the south.
Cuvée Frédéric Emile is a different Trimbach Riesling, from Grand Cru slopes above Ribeauvillé, also labelled simply Alsace.

cards.front: Trimbach's Clos Sainte Hune lies inside which Grand Cru, and does its label say so?
cards.back: The Rosacker at Hunawihr; the label names only the appellation Alsace.

cards.front: How is Trimbach's Clos Sainte Hune made, and when is it released?
cards.back: Fermented dry in stainless steel with no oak, then held in the cellar for several years before release.

questions.q: A guest reads Alsace, Riesling and Clos Ste Hune on a Trimbach label and asks why no Grand Cru appears. What do you say?
opts: The house leaves the Rosacker name off by choice
The parcel lies on the plain outside every Grand Cru
A Grand Cru label may not name Riesling
The wine is a blend, which a Grand Cru forbids
questions.exp: Clos Sainte Hune lies inside Grand Cru Rosacker, but Trimbach labels it Alsace by choice; Riesling is one of the four noble grapes every Grand Cru admits.

questions.exp: Trimbach counts from 1626; 1639 is Hugel's arrival at Riquewihr, 1898 the Faller family's purchase of Weinbach and 1947 the founding of Marcel Deiss.

wine.name: Gewurztraminer Vendange Tardive
wine.classification: Vendanges Tardives, a legal late harvest mention of the Alsace appellation, defined in 1984
wine.grapes: Gewurztraminer alone, picked late and very ripe.
wine.sites: The family's own vines on the slopes around Riquewihr, the marl and clay of the Sporen Grand Cru among them, though the label names no cru.
wine.making: Picked by hand in a late pass at or above the legal minimum ripeness, with no sugar added, the harvest declared in advance and checked by the authorities. The juice ferments slowly in the house's large old oak casks until the yeast stops of its own accord, leaving the grape's natural sweetness.
wine.glass: Lychee, rose petal and candied ginger over quince paste, orange peel and acacia honey; rich and unctuous, its sweetness held in check by a faint bitter grip at the finish rather than by acidity.
wine.ageing: Open and perfumed on release, it deepens for ten to twenty years in a good vintage, turning towards dried apricot and saffron.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small white wine glass and a modest pour, with foie gras, Munster or a fruit tart.

label.means: Late harvest of a noble grape at a set minimum sugar, with no chaptalisation; rich, or at times nearly dry.
The grape, written in Alsace without the German umlaut; Gewürz is German for spice.
The appellation; the late harvest words are a mention added to it, never an appellation of their own.

records.table: Late picked Gewurztraminer from the slopes of Riquewihr, made with no added sugar, is what Vendange Tardive means at Hugel, the family that campaigned for the law of 1984. Pour it for its lychee, rose and ginger, rich enough to meet foie gras.
records.story: The Thirty Years War had not yet ended when the Hugels came to Riquewihr in 1639, by the family's own account, and they have made wine inside its walls ever since. Their cellar keeps a great oval cask, the Sainte Catherine, made in 1715 and, as the house tells it, in use ever since. In the ripe autumns of the twentieth century the family picked overripe and noble rot grapes in separate late passes and sold them as Vendange Tardive and Sélection de Grains Nobles, words that then had no legal meaning. After the rich vintage of 1976 a son of the house led the growers' campaign for rules, and in 1984 French law defined both terms: the four noble grapes alone, a minimum sugar for each, the picking declared in advance and checked, and no sugar added. Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris must reach a higher minimum than Riesling and Muscat. Hugel long left the names of its Grand Cru slopes off its labels, so its late harvest wines speak of Riquewihr and the year rather than of a cru. When the 2021 vintage brought a compulsory sweetness mention to Alsace whites, the two late harvest terms were spared it, since each already tells the guest what the bottle holds. Every bottle is the law of 1984 at work, late picked with nothing added, its sweetness the grape's own.

others.name: Gewurztraminer Sélection de Grains Nobles
others.note: Noble rot berries picked pass by pass; always sweet, and made only in the years that allow it.

others.name: Riesling Schoelhammer
others.note: A single parcel of the Schoenenbourg slope, released only in selected years.

traps: A Vendange Tardive can finish nearly dry, while a Sélection de Grains Nobles is always sweet.
Vendange Tardive and Sélection de Grains Nobles are mentions on the Alsace appellation, limited to the four noble grapes, not appellations of their own.
Hugel's labels leave out the Grand Cru names of the Sporen and the Schoenenbourg, so a Hugel late harvest names no cru.

cards.front: What did the French law of 1984, pressed for by the Hugel family, define?
cards.back: Vendange Tardive and Sélection de Grains Nobles: noble grapes only, a minimum sugar for each, picking declared in advance and no added sugar.

cards.front: Hugel's Gewurztraminer Vendange Tardive: may the grower add sugar to the juice?
cards.back: No: chaptalisation is forbidden for both late harvest mentions, so the sweetness is the grape's own.

questions.q: A guest compares Hugel's Gewurztraminer Vendange Tardive with its Sélection de Grains Nobles. Which statement holds?
opts: Only the Sélection de Grains Nobles must always be sweet
Both must be made from botrytised berries alone
The Vendange Tardive may be chaptalised in a cool year
The Sélection de Grains Nobles may be made from Pinot Blanc
questions.exp: A Sélection de Grains Nobles is always sweet, while a Vendange Tardive may finish nearly dry; neither may be chaptalised, and both are limited to the four noble grapes.

questions.q: In which year did French law, after a campaign led by the Hugel family, define the Alsace late harvest terms?
questions.exp: Both late harvest terms were defined in 1984; 1962 is the Alsace appellation, 1975 the first Grand Cru and 2007 the admission of Kaefferkopf as the fifty-first.

records.place: Turckheim, with the Rangen at Thann, Alsace

wine.name: Riesling Rangen de Thann Clos Saint Urbain
wine.classification: Alsace Grand Cru, from the southernmost of the fifty-one sites
wine.sites: Clos Saint Urbain, the family's own parcel of the Rangen above Thann, around a chapel of the winegrowers' saint: volcanic and volcano sedimentary rock on a very steep slope above the river Thur.
wine.making: Whole bunches are pressed slowly and the juice ferments with its own yeasts in old oak foudres, for months at a time, stopping where it will. The wine then rests on its fine lees before bottling, with no new oak.
wine.glass: Smoke, struck flint and crushed dark rock over lime, quince and candied ginger; dense and powerful, at times with a touch of sweetness, and a long, almost salty finish.
wine.ageing: Smoky and closed for its first five to eight years, it then opens and lasts twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The Grand Cru above Thann, volcanic and very steep, the southernmost in Alsace.
The family's parcel inside the Rangen, named for the chapel of the winegrowers' saint.
The domaine's own sweetness scale printed on the label, not a legal category.

records.table: On the volcanic Rangen above Thann, the southernmost Grand Cru of Alsace, Zind-Humbrecht farms Clos Saint Urbain, and its Riesling smells of smoke and struck flint. It can keep a touch of sugar, and the domaine's own sweetness index on the label says how much.
records.story: Two families' vines became one domaine in 1959, when a Humbrecht grower, from a family that had tended vines south of Colmar since the seventeenth century by its own account, married a daughter of the Zind family, and the domaine took both names. In 1977 the family bought Clos Saint Urbain, a parcel of the Rangen above Thann whose steepness had left much of the hill neglected; few growers then wished to work rock so hard to farm. The Rangen was classified Grand Cru in 1983, and the clos became the domaine's southernmost wine, far from its home at Turckheim. In 1989 the founders' son became the first French winemaker to pass the Master of Wine examination. He took the domaine to very low yields, slow ferments with the grapes' own yeasts in old casks and, from the late 1990s, biodynamic farming. Because those ferments often stopped short of dryness, the domaine began printing its own sweetness index on the label, years before Alsace law made a sweetness mention compulsory with the 2021 vintage. Clos Saint Urbain puts the Rangen in one bottle: volcanic rock, a hand worked slope and a label that warns the guest how sweet the glass will be.

others.name: Pinot Gris Clos Jebsal

The Rangen is at Thann, volcanic and the southernmost Grand Cru, not a site near Colmar.

cards.front: On what rock does Zind-Humbrecht's Clos Saint Urbain grow, and above which town?
cards.back: The volcanic and volcano sedimentary rock of the Rangen, above Thann on the river Thur.

questions.q: A guest asks why Zind-Humbrecht's Rangen de Thann Clos Saint Urbain smells of smoke and struck flint. Which reason fits?
opts: Volcanic rock on the steep Rangen above Thann
New oak barrels charred before filling
Granite at the mouth of the Kaysersberg valley
Botrytis from the river mists of the plain
questions.exp: The Rangen is the volcanic Grand Cru, and its rock gives the smoky, flinty note; the domaine uses old foudres, not new oak, and granite is the Schlossberg's.

questions.q: In 1959 a marriage joined two Alsace families' vines into one domaine that took both their names. Which domaine?

Weinbach
Marcel Deiss
Trimbach

wine.name: Riesling Grand Cru Schlossberg Cuvée Sainte Catherine
wine.classification: Alsace Grand Cru, from the Schlossberg, the first site classified, in 1975
wine.sites: The domaine's parcels on the Schlossberg, the steep granite hill above Kientzheim and Kaysersberg, facing south; the walled Clos des Capucins lies at its foot.
wine.making: Made from later picked fruit and named for Saint Catherine's day, 25 November. The juice ferments with its own yeasts in the old oak foudres of the domaine's cellar and rests on its lees until bottling, with no new oak.
wine.glass: Ripe peach, lemon curd and orange zest over crushed granite and white pepper, with a hint of rose; broad and ripe yet driven by firm acidity, at times with a trace of sweetness.
wine.ageing: Charming young, it gains depth for ten to fifteen years, and a strong year keeps for twenty and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant only a young bottle, and briefly; a wide white wine glass.

label.means: The granite Grand Cru of Kaysersberg and Kientzheim, the first classified, in 1975.
A house name for later picked Riesling, after the saint's day, not a vineyard.
The walled vineyard around the domaine's house, planted by Capuchin friars.

records.table: Named for Saint Catherine's day in late November, Domaine Weinbach's Cuvée Sainte Catherine is later picked Riesling from the granite Schlossberg, the first Grand Cru of Alsace. Ripe peach and lemon curd ride on a firm spine of acidity.
records.story: In 1612, as the domaine tells it, Capuchin friars planted the walled vineyard below the Schlossberg, and the little stream that runs through it, the Weinbach, later gave the estate its name. The Revolution took the friars' clos and sold it as national property, and in 1898 the Faller family bought it. The granite hill above became the first Grand Cru of Alsace in 1975. After the death of the head of the family in 1979, his widow and their two daughters ran the domaine for more than three decades, and they built its name for ripe, perfumed wines called after the family and the saints rather than after sites: Cuvée Théo for the late husband, Cuvée Laurence, and Sainte Catherine for the saint's day in late November, when the last grapes came in. The vineyards came to be farmed biodynamically, and the women of the family made the domaine a house that a guest knows by its first names. Hence the rule its labels teach, that in Alsace a cuvée may honour a person or a saint while only the cru tells you where the grapes grew.

wine.name: Altenberg de Bergheim Grand Cru
wine.appellation: Alsace Grand Cru Altenberg de Bergheim
wine.classification: Alsace Grand Cru, one of the two whose rules admit a blend of grapes
wine.grapes: A field blend of several varieties planted together in the same rows, Riesling, Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer among them, picked and fermented as one.
wine.sites: The domaine's parcels of the Altenberg, the old hill above Bergheim, on limestone and marl with red clay, facing south.
wine.making: Every variety in a parcel is picked on the same day, pressed together and fermented slowly with its own yeasts in old oak foudres, often for many months. The wine rests long on its lees and frequently keeps some natural sugar.
wine.glass: Candied orange, quince and dried apricot over ginger, honeycomb and a salty, chalky grip; broad and textured, often a little sweet, with a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Rich and closed in its youth, it opens after five to eight years and lasts twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a large white wine glass.

label.means: The Grand Cru of Bergheim whose rules admit a blend, so the label names no grape.
One of the fifty-one Alsace Grand Cru appellations, each an appellation of its own since 2011.

records.table: No grape appears on Domaine Marcel Deiss's Altenberg de Bergheim, because the Grand Cru admits a field blend: several varieties grown side by side, picked and fermented together. Rich, textured and often a touch sweet, it tastes of the hill before any one grape.
records.story: The founder whose name the domaine carries came home to Bergheim after the Second World War and set up the domaine in 1947, selling wine by grape, as Alsace did. His grandson took charge in the 1970s and came to argue that the grape was hiding the place: the old vineyards of Alsace, he held, had been planted with many varieties together, and the great hills were known by name long before anyone sold their wine by grape. He replanted parcels with mixed varieties, farmed them biodynamically and labelled them by site alone, at first against the rules, which asked a Grand Cru for a single noble grape. The argument won ground. The rules of the Altenberg de Bergheim were rewritten to admit a blend of the hill, and Kaefferkopf, admitted in 2007 as the fifty-first Grand Cru, took blends as well. When each Grand Cru became an appellation of its own in 2011, the Altenberg kept that right in its own rules. The domaine bottles the Altenberg, the Schoenenbourg and the Mambourg as field blends, each named for its hill. The Altenberg answers an old Alsace question: a Grand Cru may name its place and no grape at all.

others.name: Schoenenbourg
others.note: The Riquewihr Grand Cru as a field blend, on marl and gypsum.

others.name: Mambourg
others.note: A field blend from the warm marl and limestone of Sigolsheim.

others.name: Burg
others.note: A lieu dit field blend that brings the domaine's argument to a wine below Grand Cru.

Altenberg de Bergheim and Kaefferkopf admit blends and Zotzenberg admits Sylvaner; the other Grand Crus ask for a single noble grape.
Complantation means co-planting in the vineyard, not blending finished wines in the cellar.

It is Riesling, which an Alsace label may leave unnamed
It is declassified wine sold outside the appellation

For the refuter to confirm on the domaine's own history page: the founder's return after the war, the grandson's taking charge in the 1970s, biodynamic farming, and the soil and aspect of the Altenberg as given.
The year the Altenberg's rules admitted the blend is the early 2000s in the author's recollection and is left out for want of a source.
The founder is named only in the house's name, for want of his dates; the grandson and his son are living and are not named.
The varieties of the blend are given as Riesling, Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer among others, since the count of varieties in the parcels could not be confirmed.
The wine is named Altenberg de Bergheim Grand Cru as the author recalls the label; the refuter may shorten it to the plan's words.
